knowledge_type_note: Terminology for a class of move, not a motif and not a principle. There is no rule that says 'sacrifice here'. The record's real content is Spielmann's CLASSIFICATION, which is what makes the word usable.

attributions.note: The Art of Sacrifice in Chess was the first systematic attempt to classify sacrifices; the sham/real division is his and remains standard.

history.notes: Sacrifices are as old as the game and no one coined the word. What is securely attributable is the CLASSIFICATION, which is Spielmann's and is read here from his own text rather than from summaries. Note he did not claim the taxonomy was objective — of the real-sacrifice subdivisions he wrote 'I have had to adopt a subjective point of view again and to proceed at times by instinct.'

development.change: Sacrificial attack treated as the natural style of play; soundness secondary.
First systematic classification: sham vs real, active vs passive, and subtypes by object.
The positional sacrifice, especially of the exchange, is developed into a standing strategic method rather than an attacking device.
Speculative sacrifices are checkable after the fact; some famous ones are refuted, and some long-doubted ones are confirmed. Practical value at the board is unaffected by either.

engine_era_note: Engines settle soundness for sham sacrifices completely and retrospectively for real ones. What they do not settle is whether a sacrifice was a good PRACTICAL decision: a line refuted by weeks of analysis was never going to be refuted by a defender under a clock. An explanation should distinguish 'objectively unsound' from 'a bad decision', which are not the same claim.

preconditions: A move gives up material that static exchange evaluation says was takeable
indicators_for: The opponent must accept, or is much worse for declining
Concrete compensation is nameable: lines opened at the king, tempi, a structural wound, a square
The line is forcing, so the consequences can be calculated
indicators_against: Material is given up with nothing nameable in return — that is a blunder, not a sacrifice
The 'sacrifice' can be declined at no cost, and the offering side is then simply worse
The compensation described is not actually present on the board
false_positive_traps: A capture the engine happens to like is not a sacrifice. The repo's own definition is the right one: material that CAN be taken and is offered anyway, measured by SEE.
An even trade is not a sacrifice.
Calling a blunder a sacrifice. The difference is whether the compensation is real and nameable — annotators decide between '!' and '?' on exactly that.

typical_plans: Open lines towards an uncastled or under-defended king
Buy two or three tempi at the critical moment
Obtain a square or colour complex the opponent can never contest
typical_moves: Nd5 and Nf5 piece sacrifices in the Sicilian
tactical_consequences: Forcing sequences that end in mate or material recovery
strategic_consequences: Converts material into a lasting positional asset that survives into the endgame

exceptions: A sham sacrifice is not really a sacrifice at all; treating it as one invites judgement where calculation was required.
A passive sacrifice can simply be declined. Not noticing that is a standard error.
An objectively unsound sacrifice can be the best practical decision against a human on a clock. Those are different claims and should not be merged.
limitations: 'Sacrifice' names what a move DOES, not whether it is good. Soundness is a separate question answered by calculation or judgement, depending on the type.
Spielmann's real-sacrifice subdivisions are explicitly subjective by his own statement.
misconceptions: That every material give-up is a sacrifice — a blunder gives up material for nothing.
That sacrifices are inherently risky. Sham sacrifices carry no risk at all; that is what makes them sham.
That a sacrifice refuted by an engine was a mistake to play. Objective soundness and practical merit are different questions.

by_level.beginner: This gives away material on purpose, to get something else — usually an attack on the king or a piece that cannot be stopped.
by_level.intermediate: A sacrifice. First ask whether the material comes back by force: if it does, calculate it and stop worrying. If it does not, you are judging the compensation instead.
by_level.advanced: Spielmann's division applies: sham if the material returns by force or mate follows, real if it does not. The two are checked by different faculties — calculation and judgement — and mixing them is the standard error.
by_level.master: Name the compensation in the currency actually obtained: tempi, king exposure, structure, squares, coordination. Note the floor as well as the ceiling — a sacrifice with a mating ceiling and a drawing floor is a different proposition from one that mates or loses.

by_depth.normal: A sacrifice: {n} points of material given up for {compensation}. The material {does / does not} come back by force, so this is a {sham / real} sacrifice.
by_depth.deep: Spielmann classified sacrifices in 1935 and the frame still holds. A sham sacrifice regains the material by force or ends in mate — no risk, and 'properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' A real sacrifice cannot be calculated out; the player relies on judgement, and 'the risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice.' The practical point is that the two are verified differently, calculation against judgement, and confusing them goes wrong in both directions. A second axis is whether the offer must be accepted or may be declined.

explanations.lesson: Before you sacrifice, ask one question first: does the material come back by force? If yes, calculate to the end and trust nothing else. If no, name what you are buying — and if you cannot name it, the move is a blunder rather than a sacrifice.

avoid: the engine refuted it so it was a mistake

definition_short: Deliberately giving up material for compensation in another currency — time, king exposure, structure, squares, or mate.
definition_long:
The voluntary surrender of material for something not measured in material. What makes the word worth having is Spielmann's division, which is still the standard frame ninety years on.

SHAM (pseudo, temporary) — the material comes back by force, with interest, or the line ends in mate. Spielmann is blunt: 'Properly speaking, there is no sacrifice, only an advantageous business deal.' He subdivides these into positional sacrifices, sacrifices for gain, and mating sacrifices. There is no risk, because the consequences were foreseen from the first.

REAL — the player 'gives up material, but is unable to calculate the consequences with accuracy; he has to rely on his judgment.' Compensation is dynamic and must be realised gradually. Spielmann's own summary: 'the risk is the hallmark of the real sacrifice.'

The division matters because THE TWO ARE CHECKED BY DIFFERENT FACULTIES. A sham sacrifice is settled by calculation and nothing else; a real one by judgement. Confusing them goes wrong in both directions — trying to calculate a real sacrifice to exhaustion, or 'judging' a sham one on intuition when a variation would have settled it.

Spielmann's second axis is ACTIVE versus PASSIVE: an active sacrifice must be accepted, a passive one may be declined without the declining side being worse. He notes the active form is 'by far the more powerful'. Wikipedia renders the same distinction as forced/non-forced, and adds that failing to notice when an offer can simply be declined is a common error.

Compensation, concretely, is some mix of: time (the initiative), king exposure, structure, squares and domination, and the destruction of the opponent's coordination.
